title: Deferred Tax Assets & Liabilities
description: Understand how temporary differences can create future taxable or deductible amounts.
html:
Future tax consequences

Temporary differences can create future taxable amounts or future deductible amounts.

This leads us to deferred tax liabilities and deferred tax assets.

Deferred Tax Liability

A taxable temporary difference generally creates a Deferred Tax Liability (DTL).

Think: more tax expected in a future period because of the reversal.

Deferred Tax Asset

A deductible temporary difference generally creates a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA).

Think: future tax deduction or tax benefit associated with the reversal.

Basic calculation

For our introductory examples, assume a single enacted tax rate applies when the temporary difference reverses.

Deferred Tax Amount = Temporary Difference × Applicable Enacted Tax Rate

DTL example

Assume a taxable temporary difference is $50,000.

Assume the enacted tax rate expected to apply when it reverses is 25%.

$50,000 × 25% = $12,500 DTL

DTA example

Assume a deductible temporary difference is $40,000.

Assume the applicable enacted tax rate is 25%.

$40,000 × 25% = $10,000 DTA

DTL

Taxable temporary difference

Future taxable amount

DTA

Deductible temporary difference

Future deductible amount

Important caution

Deferred tax accounting can become considerably more complex than simply multiplying one difference by one rate.

At CPA level, we will work with tax bases, multiple temporary differences, changes in enacted tax rates and the realizability of deferred tax assets.

For now memorize the direction

Taxable temporary difference → DTL

Deductible temporary difference → DTA

quiz.prompt: A deductible temporary difference is $80,000 and the applicable enacted tax rate is 25%. Ignoring other considerations, what deferred tax amount results?
quiz.explanation: $80,000 × 25% = $20,000. A deductible temporary difference generally gives rise to a deferred tax asset.
